beats.role_note: The game, the state the effect communicates (REWIND, the vulnerable window) and the textured object.
beats.narration_text: The game: two tin toys box on wind-up springs. The state is REWIND: a fighter cranks its key and is open, and a hit there does one and a half times the damage. That is the vulnerable window, and the tint has to say punish now. Here it is in Tharun's own screenshot from play, both fighters blue. The object is the toy box in the prop room, which gets a textured shader.

beats.role_note: Q1 what a shader does — rewind_tint.gdshader:7-8; the colour line from CHANGE-BRIEF A5.2.
beats.narration_text: Question one: what does a shader do? It is a small program the graphics card runs for every pixel it draws. Line three declares rewind amount, a number the game sets from outside. Line seven opens fragment, which runs once for each pixel of the sprite. And line eight is the colour line from the brief: mix the sprite's colour toward the blue tint, by rewind amount times strength. Claude suggested that line. Tharun typed it.

beats.role_note: Controlled-value captures beside the hand predictions (CHANGE-BRIEF A5.3, pixel-samples.txt).
beats.narration_text: The result, in real engine captures at controlled values, from a scripted-input run. Tharun predicted two pixels by hand, on paper: Bolt's chest and helmet. At zero and at one half, all twelve channels match exactly. At one, four channels read one lower, all among the five whose predictions sat exactly on a half before rounding. And at two, set from code, both pixels are pure tint. So hint range does not clamp a value set from code.

beats.role_note: The driver lines — rewind_tint_driver.gd: one material per fighter, target, move_toward × delta.
beats.narration_text: The driver feeds that number. Claude wrote it, in an agent session, from a prompt Tharun approved. Line nineteen gives each fighter its own material, so Rivet's rewind never tints Bolt. Line twenty-seven sets the target: one in REWIND, zero otherwise. Line twenty-nine moves toward it, faster going up, slower coming down, times delta, so the fade runs in game time, not frames.

beats.role_note: Q2 how a material differs from a shader — painted_tin.gdshader uniforms; toybox_fresh.tres / toybox_worn.tres.
beats.narration_text: Question two: how is a material different from a shader? The shader is the program, and it declares the knobs: painted tin, lines eight to thirteen. A material is one saved set of values for those knobs. Toybox fresh and toybox worn both point at the same shader, on line eleven, and differ on lines fifteen and sixteen: paint roughness and wear amount.

beats.role_note: One shader, two materials: shader edit vs material edit (evidence/a5/captures/toybox/edit_checks/).
beats.narration_text: The proof is an edit test. Tharun changed the shader's u v scale default from two point five to six. Both boxes changed; the castle did not. Then, with the shader restored, he changed only the worn material's wear amount, from point five five to point two. Only the worn box changed, mostly bare metal back to red paint. Edit the shader, and every material follows. Edit a material, and one object changes.

beats.role_note: Q3 why a texture is information — painted_tin.gdshader:3-5 hints; line 20 roughness as the wear mask.
beats.narration_text: Question three: why is a texture information, not just a picture? Painted tin samples three images of Poly Haven's Metal Plate, by Rob Tuytel, released C C zero. Line three is colour, marked source colour, so Godot decodes it from s R G B. Line four is a normal map: its pixels store directions, not colours. Line five is roughness, plain numbers. And line twenty turns that roughness into the wear mask: where the plate is rough, the paint has worn through.

beats.role_note: The hint experiment, predicted vs measured (hint_quads.png, hint-samples.txt; CHANGE-BRIEF A5.4).
beats.narration_text: The hint experiment makes that visible. One three-pixel P N G, values sixty-four, one twenty-eight and one ninety-two, on two quads. The top quad samples it as colour, the bottom as data. Tharun predicted, by hand: the top shows the file unchanged; the bottom shows one thirty-seven, one eighty-eight and two twenty-five. Measured: exactly those six numbers. Same bytes, different meaning, and only the hint decides.

beats.role_note: Q4 the Godot shading language — standard_generated.gdshader lines 7 and 19 (annotated by Tharun) beside painted_tin.gdshader lines 3 and 4; shader_type, hints, built-ins (LANGUAGE-NOTES.md).
beats.narration_text: Question four: what is the Godot shading language? A G L S L-style language with the plumbing done for you. Shader type picks the pipeline: canvas item for the sprite, spatial for the box. Hints tell the engine how to feed a uniform, and built-ins like COLOR and ALBEDO arrive ready. On the left, the shader Godot generated from a standard material, with Tharun's notes. Line seven reads albedo as colour; line nineteen reads the normal map as data. On the right, the same jobs in painted tin, lines three and four.

beats.role_note: What the tests proved: counts and the three mutations (evidence/a5/mutations/, TEST-REPORT "Assignment 5").
beats.narration_text: What the tests proved. Test rewind tint: fifty of fifty checks at thirty, sixty and one hundred forty-four frames per second, sampled every frame through real input. Test materials: fifty-five of fifty-five, and again after deleting the import cache. The existing suites still pass: twenty-five checks with zero failed, and the props check, PASS. Then Tharun broke the shaders three ways, restoring them each time. A deleted semicolon: five failures. A renamed uniform: two. Source colour removed from line three: one. Each was caught, but only by the uniform-list and source checks; the driver's own checks kept passing.

beats.role_note: What no headless run can show (evidence/a5/headless-facts.txt; TEST-REPORT A5-13).
beats.narration_text: And what no headless run can show. The headless probe sets rewind amount to two and reads back two: it stores the number and says nothing about a pixel. Headless runs draw no image at all. Only the windowed capture showed that two meant pure blue, and only Tharun's eyes judged the look.

beats.role_note: Human and AI contributions exactly as SOURCES.md "Who did what (A5)", shown verbatim on screen.
beats.narration_text: Who did what, as SOURCES dot m d records it. Tharun accepted Claude's proposed design decisions and material plan, and computed the pixel, contrast and hint predictions by hand. He wrote the failure cases and short answers, typed all three shaders from Claude's recorded suggestions, ran the three mutations, reviewed the audit, converted the material in the editor, made both edits, took the OS screenshot and playtested. Claude proposed the design and material plan, set up the textures, ran the agent sessions that wrote the driver and test, fixed two test bugs, wrote the probes, builders and capture tools, ran the audit, made and measured every capture, and drafted the docs.

beats.role_note: VERDICT — checked by numbers / by eye, agent mistakes caught (A5-10), uncertain (M5, start delay), one next step; revision shown.
beats.narration_text: The verdict, at game revision two e six nine four six d. Checked by numbers: the fades, retrigger, both pauses and one material per fighter, at three frame rates; and eighteen hand predictions, fourteen exact and four off by one. Checked by eye: Tharun's look at the captures and in play. Six agent mistakes were caught, among them a test that read the frame rate from arguments the engine had already consumed. Still uncertain: painted tin never writes metallic, so worn metal may read as grey paint; and REWIND starts on the sixty hertz physics tick, so the fade can begin up to a sixtieth of a second after the press. One next step: write metallic from the wear mask, then sweep and look again.
